content_voiceover: Retinoblastoma arises from photoreceptor elements in the inner retinal layer, and the classic presenting sign, shown in the photo here, is leukocoria, a white pupillary reflex often first noticed on a flash photograph, which is why parents frequently bring this up themselves. Diagnosis is confirmed by fundoscopic exam. Molecularly, retinoblastoma follows Knudson's two hit hypothesis, requiring biallelic loss of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene. About twenty five percent of cases are bilateral or multifocal and heritable, meaning the patient carries a germline RB1 mutation, while the remaining seventy five percent are unilateral and mostly nonhereditary, arising from two somatic hits in one eye. A high yield related entity is trilateral retinoblastoma, which is bilateral retinoblastoma plus a separate intracranial PNET, most commonly a pineoblastoma, with about a quarter of these intracranial tumors located in the suprasellar or parasellar region instead. Treatment follows the guiding philosophy of saving life while preserving useful vision whenever possible, using systemic chemotherapy, intra-ophthalmic artery chemotherapy for localized delivery, local therapies such as laser or cryotherapy, radiotherapy, and enucleation, surgical removal of the eye, reserved for advanced or refractory disease.
keypoints: Leukocoria, white pupillary reflex, is the classic presenting sign of retinoblastoma
Retinoblastoma requires biallelic loss of RB1, following the two hit hypothesis
Twenty five percent are bilateral and heritable, seventy five percent unilateral and nonhereditary
Trilateral retinoblastoma equals bilateral RB plus intracranial PNET, usually pineoblastoma
keypoint_voiceover: Remember retinoblastoma by its hallmark sign, leukocoria, and its genetics, biallelic RB1 loss following the two hit hypothesis, with bilateral disease being the heritable form. And know trilateral retinoblastoma, bilateral RB plus an intracranial PNET, most often a pineoblastoma.
